name.text: Determining trigonometric ratios in different quadrants

questiontext.text:
The angle \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) is in standard position: it is measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. Its terminal side meets the unit circle (centre \(O\), radius \(1\)) at the point \(P\), as shown in the diagram.

Use the unit circle to find the exact values of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\).

(a) \(\sin {@theta@}^\circ = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
(b) \(\cos {@theta@}^\circ = \) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The point \(P\) where the terminal side meets the unit circle has coordinates \((\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\). The reference angle gives the size of each coordinate, and the quadrant gives its sign.

Step 1: find the quadrant. \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) lies in Quadrant {@quadname@}[[if test="is(quadrant=2)"]], between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\)[[/if]][[if test="is(quadrant=3)"]], between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\)[[/if]][[if test="is(quadrant=4)"]], between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\)[[/if]].

Step 2: find the reference angle \(\alpha\). The reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the \(x\)-axis. [[if test="is(quadrant=2)"]]In Quadrant II, \(\alpha = 180^\circ - \theta = 180^\circ - {@theta@}^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quadrant=3)"]]In Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \theta - 180^\circ = {@theta@}^\circ - 180^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quadrant=4)"]]In Quadrant IV, \(\alpha = 360^\circ - \theta = 360^\circ - {@theta@}^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]]

Step 3: use the exact values for the reference angle. From the special triangles,

\[ \sin {@ref_angle@}^\circ = {@sin_ref@}, \qquad \cos {@ref_angle@}^\circ = {@cos_ref@}. \]

These are the sizes of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\), without their signs.

Step 4: decide the signs from the quadrant. In Quadrant {@quadname@}, \(P\) is [[if test="is(quadrant=4)"]]to the right of the \(y\)-axis, so \(\cos\theta\) (the \(x\)-coordinate) is positive,[[else]]to the left of the \(y\)-axis, so \(\cos\theta\) (the \(x\)-coordinate) is negative,[[/if]] and [[if test="is(quadrant=2)"]]above the \(x\)-axis, so \(\sin\theta\) (the \(y\)-coordinate) is positive.[[else]]below the \(x\)-axis, so \(\sin\theta\) (the \(y\)-coordinate) is negative.[[/if]]

Step 5: write down the values.

\[ \sin {@theta@}^\circ = {@sin_theta@}, \qquad \cos {@theta@}^\circ = {@cos_theta@}. \]

In the diagram, the reference angle \(\alpha\) is shown in green. The right-angled triangle has hypotenuse \(OP = 1\). Its horizontal side is the size of \(\cos\theta\) and its vertical side is the size of \(\sin\theta\); the quadrant decides their signs.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\). In Quadrant {@quadname@}, is \(P\) above or below the \(x\)-axis?
That is the value of \(\cos\theta\), not \(\sin\theta\). On the unit circle, \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\).

node.description: Right sign, sin and cos of the reference angle mixed up

truefeedback.text: Your sign is right, but the size is wrong: you may have used the cosine of the reference angle instead of its sine. Find the reference angle, then check which of its sine and cosine is the larger.

falsefeedback.text: Find the reference angle (the acute angle between the terminal side and the \(x\)-axis) and use its exact sine value from the special triangles. Then use the quadrant of \(\theta\) to decide the sign: \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\).

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\). In Quadrant {@quadname@}, is \(P\) to the left or the right of the \(y\)-axis?
That is the value of \(\sin\theta\), not \(\cos\theta\). On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\).
